transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because since we put in a brighter mirror in our bathroom, I keep noticing the skin around my cheeks and jaw. It looks uneven, or sort of saggy, to me. My husband says he really can’t see what I mean, but I keep seeing it.
On an average day, about how many hours would you say you spend thinking about or checking your skin in the mirror?

Maybe an hour or so total, mostly in the mornings. I’ll check my face from different angles and put on extra makeup before I go to the courthouse. Then sometimes during the day I notice myself comparing my face to women at work, or I’ll avoid casual pictures if I’m feeling bad about it.

When your husband tells you he doesn't see what you're describing, is there any part of you that considers he might be right, or do you feel completely certain that the flaw is really there exactly as you see it?
I mean, I know he may not be seeing it the way I do. Sometimes I wonder if I’m focusing on it too much, but when I look in the mirror it still seems pretty obvious to me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistent preoccupation with a perceived flaw in her skin (unevenness/sagging) that is not observable or only slight to others (per husband's report), along with repetitive behaviors including mirror checking, camouflaging with makeup, comparing her appearance to others, and avoidance of photographs. She spends over an hour daily on these behaviors. Insight is fair—she acknowledges she may be overly focused but still perceives the flaw as real. This constellation of symptoms is most consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder with fair insight (F45.22), rather than a delusional variant (poor/absent insight) or a personality disorder or generalized anxiety presentation.
